node.title: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems

questions.stem: Which gas, along with oxides of nitrogen, is mainly responsible for acid rain?
options: Sulphur dioxide
Oxygen, which makes up about a fifth of the air
Helium, an inert gas lighter than air
Nitrogen gas itself, the main gas in the air
questions.explanation: Burning of coal and oil in industries, power plants and vehicles releases sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. These dissolve in rain water to form acids and cause acid rain, which harms crops, soil, water bodies and buildings. Oxygen, helium and nitrogen gas do not cause it.

optionRationale.2: Oxygen is a normal part of the air and does not form acid rain.
optionRationale.3: Helium is an inert gas and takes no part in acid rain.
optionRationale.4: Nitrogen gas is inert in the air; it is its oxides that cause acid rain.

questions.objective: Identify the cause of acid rain

questions.stem: The loudness of noise is measured in
options: Hertz
Lux
Decibels
Pascals
questions.explanation: Noise pollution is measured in decibels (dB), which is the unit of sound intensity level. Hertz measures the frequency of sound, lux measures illumination, and pascal is a unit of pressure.

optionRationale.1: Hertz measures frequency and not loudness.
optionRationale.4: Pascal is a unit of pressure.

questions.objective: Recall the unit of noise measurement

questions.stem: Eutrophication of a lake is mainly caused by
options: excess silt brought down from the mountains by the rivers in the monsoon season
run-off carrying fertilisers and sewage rich in nutrients
a sudden fall in the temperature of the water during the winter months
the entry of sea water into the lake
questions.explanation: Fertilisers and sewage add nutrients to water. These make algae grow rapidly, and when the algae die and decay, bacteria use up the dissolved oxygen so that fish and other life die. This enrichment by nutrients is called eutrophication.

optionRationale.1: Silt makes water muddy but is not the nutrient enrichment behind eutrophication.
optionRationale.3: A temperature fall does not cause eutrophication.
optionRationale.4: Sea water entry causes salinity, not nutrient enrichment.

questions.stem: The ravines of the Chambal valley are mainly the result of
options: strong winds carrying away dry topsoil in a desert region over many years
waterlogging in canal-irrigated fields that raises salts to the surface
shifting cultivation in the north-eastern hills
running water cutting deep channels in loose soil (gully erosion)
questions.explanation: In regions with loose soil and heavy rain, running water cuts deep channels called gullies. As the gullies deepen and spread, the land breaks into ravines, as in the Chambal valley. Wind erosion, waterlogging and shifting cultivation produce different forms of degradation.

optionRationale.1: Wind erosion is typical of arid regions.
optionRationale.2: Waterlogging causes salinity and alkalinity in irrigated areas.
optionRationale.3: Shifting cultivation belongs to the hills and forests of the north-east.

questions.stem: Match the type of pollution in List-I with its main source in List-II.

right: I. Hot water discharged by power plants
III. Excess pesticides and dumped industrial waste
IV. Burning of coal and other fossil fuels

options: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III
A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
questions.explanation: Noise comes from loudspeakers, traffic and machines. Thermal pollution of rivers results from hot water discharged by power plants. Soil pollution comes from excess pesticides and dumped industrial waste, and air pollution from burning coal and other fossil fuels. So A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

optionRationale.1: This code swaps noise and thermal pollution sources.
optionRationale.2: This code swaps the sources of soil pollution and air pollution.

questions.objective: Match pollution types with their sources

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Slums are often found in the large cities of developing countries.
Reason (R): Burning fossil fuels in vehicles adds pollutants to urban air.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true but (R) is false.
(A) is false but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Slums develop in big cities of developing countries where many poor migrants cannot afford housing, so A is true. Burning fossil fuels in vehicles does pollute urban air, so R is true. But air pollution does not explain why slums develop, so R is not the explanation.

optionRationale.1: Vehicle pollution has no causal link with the rise of slums.
optionRationale.3: R is true, so the option calling it false is wrong.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so the option calling it false is wrong.

questions.objective: Separate unrelated true statements about urban problems

questions.stem:
Consider the statements on migration.
A. Rural-urban migration is shaped by both push and pull factors.
B. Money sent home by migrants (remittances) helps rural families.
C. Migration never affects the infrastructure of the city.
Which statements are correct?
options: A and C only
B and C only
A and B only
A, B and C
questions.explanation: Migration results from push factors in the village and pull factors in the city, so A is correct. Remittances sent home support families, so B is correct. Statement C is false because rapid migration puts heavy pressure on housing, water, transport and other services in the city.

optionRationale.1: C is false, so any option with C is wrong.
optionRationale.2: C is false, so this pair is wrong.
optionRationale.4: C is false, so all three cannot be correct.

questions.stem: Large cities are usually warmer than the surrounding countryside mainly because
options: buildings and roads hold heat, vegetation is scarce, and vehicles and machines add heat
cities always lie at a much higher altitude than the countryside, so they get more sunshine
rain falls only over villages
the sun's rays are stronger over cities
questions.explanation: Concrete, asphalt and buildings absorb heat by day and release it slowly, there are few trees to cool the air, and vehicles, industries and air conditioners give off more heat. This produces the urban heat island effect. Altitude and sun strength do not explain it.

optionRationale.2: Many warm cities lie at low altitude, so altitude is not the cause.
optionRationale.3: Rain falls over cities as well as villages.
optionRationale.4: The sun's rays are the same over a city and the nearby countryside.

questions.objective: Explain the urban heat island effect

questions.stem: A city produces 800 tonnes of waste a day. With segregation, 35 per cent is recycled and 25 per cent is composted. How many tonnes a day remain for landfill?
questions.explanation: Recycled plus composted waste is 35 + 25 = 60 per cent, so 40 per cent remains for landfill. Then 40/100 x 800 = 320 tonnes a day. The figure 480 is the amount recycled and composted, not the amount left.

optionRationale.1: 280 is the recycled amount alone (35 per cent of 800).
optionRationale.3: 480 tonnes is the amount recycled and composted, 60 per cent.
optionRationale.4: 520 tonnes is 65 per cent of 800, not the landfill share.

questions.objective: Compute landfill load after recycling and composting

questions.stem:
Consider the statements on land degradation.
A. Soil erosion removes fertile topsoil.
B. Shelterbelts of trees reduce wind erosion in dry regions.
C. Terracing on slopes increases the speed of run-off.
D. Excessive use of chemical fertilisers can degrade soil quality.
Which statements are correct?
options: A and C only
B and C only
A, B and C only
A, B and D only
questions.explanation: Erosion strips fertile topsoil, shelterbelts slow the wind in dry areas, and excessive chemical fertilisers can harm soil quality, so A, B and D are correct. Statement C is false because terraces slow down run-off and reduce erosion on slopes.

optionRationale.1: C is false, and this option leaves out B and D.
optionRationale.2: C is false, so this option cannot be right.
optionRationale.3: C is false, and D is also correct, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on causes and remedies of land degradation

questions.stem: Why is in-situ upgrading of a slum generally preferred to its forced demolition?
options: It improves housing and services where residents already live and work
It moves all residents far away from their places of work and their sources of income
It prevents any further migration to the city by law
It removes water and sanitation so that people leave
questions.explanation: Residents of a slum usually have jobs, schools and social ties close by. Upgrading provides water, toilets, drains and secure tenure in the same place, so conditions improve without loss of livelihood. Demolition only shifts the problem or moves people far from work.

optionRationale.2: Moving people far from work harms livelihoods and is what upgrading avoids.
optionRationale.3: Migration cannot be stopped by a law, and upgrading is not a migration law.
optionRationale.4: Upgrading adds services; it does not remove them.

options: people who suffer from pollution must pay the government for the harm they face
only the government pays for all clean-up work, whoever caused the pollution
those who cause pollution should bear the cost of damage and its control
large industries are free to pollute
questions.explanation: Under the polluter pays principle, those responsible for pollution bear the cost of cleaning it up, compensating the victims and preventing further harm. This gives them a reason to reduce pollution. It does not make victims pay or free large industries to pollute.

optionRationale.1: The victims of pollution are not the ones who pay.
optionRationale.2: The principle places the cost on the polluter, not only on the government.
optionRationale.4: It does not allow anyone to pollute freely.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Untreated sewage discharged into a river raises its Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD).
Reason (R): Sewage contains no organic matter, so micro-organisms have nothing to decompose.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true but (R) is false.
(A) is false but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Sewage is rich in organic matter. Micro-organisms decomposing it use up dissolved oxygen, so the oxygen demand of the water rises, making A true. R is false because sewage contains a great deal of organic matter, which is exactly what raises the demand.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
optionRationale.2: R is false, so the option claiming both are true is wrong.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so the option calling it false is wrong.

questions.objective: Relate sewage to oxygen demand in water

questions.stem: Which is a likely result of deforestation on steep hill slopes?
options: Faster run-off, soil erosion and landslides
Slower run-off and more soil formation
A higher level of groundwater on the slope
Reduced danger of floods in the valleys
questions.explanation: Trees hold the soil with their roots and slow the fall of rain. When they are removed from steep slopes, water runs off faster, the soil is washed away and landslides become more likely. Floods in the valleys below may also increase.

optionRationale.2: Run-off becomes faster, not slower, after tree cover is lost.
optionRationale.3: Less water soaks in, so groundwater is not raised.
optionRationale.4: Faster run-off tends to increase flood danger below.

questions.objective: State the effects of deforestation on slopes

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a source of water pollution?
options: Untreated sewage
Industrial effluents
Run-off carrying fertilisers and pesticides
Planting trees along the river bank
questions.explanation: Sewage, industrial effluents and run-off carrying fertilisers and pesticides all add harmful substances to water. Planting trees on the bank, on the other hand, holds the soil and filters run-off, so it helps protect water and is not a source of pollution.

optionRationale.1: Untreated sewage is a major source of water pollution.
optionRationale.2: Industrial effluents carry chemicals into water.
optionRationale.3: Farm run-off adds fertilisers and pesticides to water.

questions.stem: Smog is most likely to build up over a city on a cold, still winter morning because
options: strong winds disperse the smoke upwards and carry it far from the city
a temperature inversion traps smoke and pollutants near the ground
heavy rain washes the air clean and removes pollutants before they can build up
warm air rises freely and carries the pollutants high
questions.explanation: On a cold, calm morning the air near the ground can be cooler than the air above it, which is a temperature inversion. Smoke and pollutants cannot rise and spread, so they collect with fog near the ground as smog. Wind, rain and rising warm air would clear the pollutants.

optionRationale.1: Strong winds would disperse pollutants, but the morning is still.
optionRationale.3: Rain would wash out pollutants, but there is no rain in the case.
optionRationale.4: Free rising of warm air would carry pollutants away, which is the opposite of an inversion.

questions.stem: A state has 60 million people, 20 per cent of them urban. After a decade the state has 72 million people, 25 per cent of them urban. By what percentage did its urban population increase?
options: 25 per cent
50 per cent
60 per cent
5 per cent
questions.explanation: Urban population at first = 0.20 x 60 = 12 million. Later = 0.25 x 72 = 18 million. The rise is 6 million, and 6/12 x 100 = 50 per cent. The 5 is the rise in the urban share, in percentage points, and not the growth of the urban population.

optionRationale.1: 25 per cent is the new urban share, not the growth.
optionRationale.3: 6 million out of 12 million is not 60 per cent.
optionRationale.4: 5 is the change in the urban share in percentage points.

questions.stem: Which combination of measures best controls land degradation in a hilly, rain-fed region?
options: Heavy grazing and clearing the slopes for crops
Ploughing up and down the slope and burning crop residue
Growing a single crop and leaving the soil bare after harvest
Contour bunding or terracing, afforestation and check dams
questions.explanation: On slopes, terraces and contour bunds slow run-off, trees hold the soil, and check dams stop gullies from growing. Together they reduce erosion in a rain-fed hilly region. Overgrazing, ploughing up and down the slope and leaving soil bare increase the loss of soil.

optionRationale.1: Overgrazing and clearing slopes cause degradation.
optionRationale.2: Ploughing up and down the slope speeds run-off, and burning residue harms soil.
optionRationale.3: Bare soil after harvest is open to erosion.

questions.objective: Select suitable conservation measures for hills
